screens.title: Advanced VPC Design and Network Segmentation
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll build a practical mental model for enterprise network design on AWS. You will learn why a flat single-VPC model breaks down as organizations grow, and how a hub-and-spoke Transit Gateway architecture reduces operational complexity while supporting isolation. We'll also unpack two complementary firewall primitives: Security Groups, which are stateful and instance-focused, and Network ACLs, which are stateless and subnet-focused. Throughout, you'll see concrete examples: separate VPCs for dev, staging, and production; a shared services VPC that exposes central services; and an isolation pattern that prevents direct east–west traffic between sensitive environments. I will highlight common mistakes — for example, relying only on Security Groups for subnet-level controls or creating a peering mesh that becomes unmanageable — and show how route tables and Transit Gateway route table associations and propagations enforce intended connectivity. By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain when Transit Gateway is the right choice, how to combine NACLs and Security Groups for defense-in-depth, and what checks to run after a change to avoid breaking DNS or time synchronization. Think about one network you manage now and whether a centralized hub could simplify its routing; that's the lens we use here.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use when designing enterprise networks on AWS. First, you will learn to design multi-VPC architectures that provide clear isolation boundaries while remaining scalable. That means assigning VPCs roles, choosing CIDR ranges, and planning connectivity so teams don't create ad hoc peering meshes. Second, you will implement hub-and-spoke network topologies using AWS Transit Gateway. You will understand attachments, route tables, associations and propagations so the hub enforces traffic flows. Third, you will differentiate Security Groups and Network ACLs: when to use stateful, instance-level controls versus stateless, subnet-level deny-or-allow policies, and how to combine them for defense-in-depth. Fourth, you will identify and mitigate common networking challenges in complex VPC environments, such as unintended route propagation, broken DNS or NTP after policy changes, and overly permissive or overly fragmented VPC designs. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify you can design, implement, and validate secure, scalable networks. As you work through the hands-on scenario later, use these objectives to check that your architecture both enforces isolation and supports required shared services. screens.title: Multi-VPC Architecture: purpose and planning
screens.narratorSegment: Multi-VPC architecture is the deliberate use of multiple Virtual Private Clouds to provide isolation, organizational boundaries, and scale. Practically, that means creating VPCs with specific roles — for example production, development, and shared services — and assigning CIDR ranges so they do not overlap. A clear purpose for each VPC matters because it reduces accidental exposure; a production VPC will carry stricter rules than a development VPC. When planning CIDRs, reserve headroom for future subnets and avoid ranges that will conflict with on-prem networks if you plan to connect via VPN or Direct Connect. A common misconception is that more VPCs always equal better isolation; too many tiny VPCs without a connectivity strategy creates operational overhead. Conversely, one very large VPC can expose unrelated teams to risk and complicate compliance. A practical rule of thumb is to balance organizational boundaries with manageability: group tightly coupled workloads together, separate sensitive workloads into their own VPCs, and document CIDR allocations centrally. Example: allocate 10.1.0.0/16 to production, 10.2.0.0/16 to development, and 10.3.0.0/16 to shared services, leaving room to subnet them per availability zone. Key takeaway: design VPCs for clear purpose and future connectivity, not for ad hoc convenience. How would you split responsibilities across VPCs in your environment?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Multi-VPC Planning
Definition

What is Multi-VPC Architecture?

Using multiple VPCs to isolate workloads by role, sensitivity, or organizational boundary while enabling controlled connectivity between them.

Concrete example
Prod: 10.1.0.0/16 with strict controls. Dev: 10.2.0.0/16 for experimentation. Shared: 10.3.0.0/16 for Active Directory and logging services.
Common mistake
Creating many tiny VPCs without a connectivity plan results in peering complexity and operational overhead.
Key Takeaway

Define VPC purpose first, then plan CIDR blocks and connectivity to avoid rework.

Planning Checklist
  • Assign a clear role to each VPC and document it.
  • Reserve CIDR blocks with future growth in mind and avoid overlaps with on-prem.
  • Consider where shared services will live and whether a shared-services VPC is needed.
  • Decide connectivity strategy up-front: Transit Gateway, peering, or Direct Connect.
Analogy
Think of each VPC as a separate office floor. Some floors need controlled shared facilities; others must remain isolated for compliance.

screens.title: VPC Peering vs Transit Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: VPC peering is a lightweight way to connect two VPCs directly. It's easy to set up and useful for a small number of connections. But peering is non-transitive: if VPC A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B without an explicit peering connection. That non-transitive nature creates a combinatorial problem as you add VPCs. For N VPCs a full mesh requires N times N minus one over two peering links, and each new peering requires route table changes in both endpoints. In contrast, AWS Transit Gateway provides a central hub. Each VPC attaches to the Transit Gateway as a spoke, and the Transit Gateway manages inter-VPC routing with route tables, associations, and propagations. This is more scalable and simplifies policy enforcement. A misconception is that Transit Gateway automatically opens all communications; it does not. You still control connectivity via Transit Gateway route tables and VPC route table entries. Example: with three VPCs — prod, dev, shared-services — you can attach all three to a TGW and use two TGW route tables to allow shared-services to reach both prod and dev, while preventing direct traffic between prod and dev. Key takeaway: use peering for a few pairwise connections, and choose Transit Gateway when you need scale, central policy, and transitive connectivity management.

keyIdea.title: Scale vs simplicity
keyIdea.text: Peering is simple for few VPCs. Transit Gateway centralizes routing and scales cleanly when many VPCs must interconnect.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Peering vs TGW
VPC Peering
Good for a small number of pairwise connections that do not require transitive routing. Easy to configure but becomes hard to manage at scale.
Pros
  • Low operational overhead for few links.
  • No central gateway cost.
Cons
Non-transitive and scales poorly; route proliferation and management overhead grow quickly.
AWS Transit Gateway
A central transit hub that attaches VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect. Simplifies routing and centralizes policy enforcement using TGW route tables.
Pros
  • Scales to many VPCs with clear route management.
  • Supports central route tables to control transitive flows.
Note
Transit Gateway adds a central control plane; you still must configure route tables correctly to enforce isolation.
Key Takeaway

Choose Transit Gateway when you need scale and central policy. Reserve peering for small, static relationships.

screens.title: Transit Gateway: hub, attachments, and route tables
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Transit Gateway is a central hub where VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect gateways attach as spokes. Each attachment represents a connection between the Transit Gateway and a VPC or on-prem gateway. The gateway itself contains route tables; you create associations and propagations to control which attachments learn or receive which routes. Associations link attachments to a specific TGW route table, and propagation advertises routes from an attachment into a route table. This design allows you to create multiple TGW route tables for different traffic domains. For example, create a SharedServices-TGW-RT that propagates the shared-services attachment and associates that attachment with the table so the shared service is reachable. Create an Isolation-TGW-RT that associates prod and dev attachments, but only propagates routes to the shared-services attachment so prod and dev cannot reach each other directly. A common misconception is that attaching a VPC to the TGW automatically grants full connectivity; it does not. You must update both the TGW route table and the VPC route table to direct traffic to the Transit Gateway for inter-VPC communication. Example: to expose shared services to both spokes, propagate shared-services routes and add static routes for prod and dev CIDRs in the SharedServices-TGW-RT. Key takeaway: the combination of associations and propagations gives you flexible, central traffic control.

keyIdea.title: Associations & propagations
keyIdea.text: Use TGW route tables with associations and propagations to selectively share routes between spokes and the hub.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Transit Gateway Internals
Key parts
  • Attachments: connections between TGW and VPCs or on-prem endpoints.
  • Route tables: control which routes are visible between attachments.
  • Associations & propagations: decide who learns which routes.
Concrete setup example
Two TGW route tables: SharedServices-TGW-RT and Isolation-TGW-RT. Associate shared-services with the shared table and propagate its routes. Associate prod and dev with the isolation table but only propagate shared-services into it so prod and dev do not see each other's CIDRs directly.
Operational notes
  • Update VPC route tables to point to the TGW for destination CIDRs you want reached via the hub.
  • Static TGW routes may be necessary to reach specific CIDRs if you do not rely on propagation.
  • Use separate TGW route tables for different policy domains to avoid accidental cross-talk.
Misconception
Attaching equals access. In reality, route table configuration drives access, not the attachment alone.
Key Takeaway

Associations and propagations let you selectively expose routes between spokes and the hub — plan TGW route tables by traffic domain.

screens.title: Configuring TGW route tables and VPC routes
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring Transit Gateway routing is a four-step process you should treat as a deliberate workflow. Step one: create the Transit Gateway and attach each VPC by creating Transit Gateway attachments; each attachment must include subnet IDs from the VPC. Step two: create TGW route tables for the traffic patterns you require — for example, SharedServices-TGW-RT and Isolation-TGW-RT. Step three: associate attachments with the appropriate TGW route table and configure route propagations so routes from attachments appear where they should. Propagation is what advertises a spoke's CIDR into a TGW route table. Step four: update the route tables within each VPC to direct inter-VPC traffic to the Transit Gateway. If you forget this step, the TGW will not be used even though the attachment exists. A common pitfall is misconfiguring associations so attachments end up in the wrong TGW table, accidentally enabling transitive flows. Example flow: attach prod, dev, and shared-services; associate prod and dev to Isolation-TGW-RT; propagate shared-services into SharedServices-TGW-RT and add static routes to prod and dev CIDRs in SharedServices-TGW-RT. Finally, test connectivity using controlled probes and validate DNS resolution. Key takeaway: follow the attach, table, associate, propagate, and VPC-route update sequence to avoid partial connectivity.

keyIdea.title: TGW routing workflow
keyIdea.text: Attach VPCs, create TGW route tables, set associations and propagations, then update VPC route tables for inter-VPC traffic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › TGW Configuration Steps
Step-by-step
  1. Create Transit Gateway and attachments for each VPC.
  2. Create TGW route tables for separate traffic domains.
  3. Associate attachments and configure propagations.
  4. Update each VPC route table to send inter-VPC traffic to the TGW.
  5. Test connectivity and validate DNS/NTP.
Example configuration
SharedServices-TGW-RT: propagate shared-services attachment; add static TGW routes for prod and dev CIDRs. Isolation-TGW-RT: associate prod and dev attachments and propagate the shared-services attachment selectively so prod and dev cannot reach one another.
Check list before go-live
  • Correct associations and propagations in TGW route tables.
  • VPC route tables updated to use TGW for target CIDRs.
  • DNS and NTP still reachable after route changes.
Key Takeaway

Follow the sequence exactly and validate each step to avoid incomplete or unsafe connectivity changes.

screens.title: Security Groups — stateful instance-level firewall
screens.narratorSegment: Security Groups are a stateful virtual firewall applied to network interfaces and instances. When you allow inbound traffic on a port, the return traffic is automatically allowed back out — you do not need explicit outbound rules for responses unless you have tightened outbound policies. Security Groups are permissive by design: you allow specific traffic and everything else is implicitly denied. This makes them ideal for instance-level protection where you want granular control, for example allowing inbound TCP 80 and 443 to web servers. A common mistake is using Security Groups as the only line of defense for subnet-level isolation; they protect instances but do not replace subnet filters when compliance requires deny-by-default at the boundary. Best practice: attach Security Groups that allow minimal required ports and, when possible, reference other Security Groups rather than IPs for tighter intra-VPC controls. Example: web server SG allows 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0, and database SG allows MySQL from the web server SG ID only. Key takeaway: use Security Groups for precise, stateful instance protections and pair them with NACLs for broader subnet-level controls when needed.

keyIdea.title: Security Groups
keyIdea.text: Use stateful, instance-level Security Groups for precise allow rules and reference-based permissions between tiers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Security Groups
Behavior

Stateful, instance-level firewall. Inbound allow implies return traffic is allowed. Default denies unless explicitly permitted.

Example configuration
Web SG: inbound TCP 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0. DB SG: inbound TCP 3306 from the Web SG's Security Group ID only.
Best practices
  • Reference Security Group IDs for intra-VPC access rather than raw IPs when possible.
  • Keep rules minimal and specific to required ports and sources.
  • Use descriptive names and tags for auditability.
Misconception
Security Groups are sufficient for subnet-level isolation. They are instance-focused and should be paired with NACLs when subnet boundaries must be enforced.
Key Takeaway

Security Groups are your fine-grained, stateful controls for instances; use them to express least privilege between tiers.

screens.title: Network ACLs — stateless subnet-level filtering
screens.narratorSegment: Network Access Control Lists are stateless filters applied at the subnet boundary. They evaluate rules in numeric order from lowest to highest, and they support both allow and deny rules. Because they are stateless, you must create both inbound and outbound rules for request and response traffic. NACLs are deny-by-default when newly created, requiring explicit allows for everything you want. This makes them useful as a coarse-grained 'moat' around a subnet, especially for regulatory workloads that demand strong subnet-level boundaries. For example, to allow web traffic into a public subnet you would add inbound rules for TCP ports 80 and 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and outbound rules permitting ephemeral ports so the web server can respond. For a database subnet, you might add an inbound rule that allows only the application's subnet CIDR on the database port and deny everything else. A common mistake is misordering NACL rules or forgetting corresponding outbound entries, which will break connections unexpectedly. Use NACLs to enforce broad deny/allow policies and Security Groups to handle instance-level stateful controls. Key takeaway: NACLs provide a coarse, stateless defense at the subnet perimeter and are ideal for compliance-driven controls.

keyIdea.title: NACL characteristics
keyIdea.text: Stateless, ordered rules at the subnet boundary. Use for coarse-grained filtering and deny-by-default compliance requirements.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Network ACLs
Behavior

Stateless subnet-level firewall. Rules are evaluated in order; both inbound and outbound must be explicitly allowed for two-way traffic.

Example
Allow inbound TCP 80/443 from internet; allow outbound ephemeral ports 1024–65535 so the web server can send responses.
Best practices
  • Use NACLs to implement deny-by-default subnet boundaries for compliance workloads.
  • Order rules carefully and include necessary ephemeral outbound allowances.
  • Test changes in staging to avoid breaking critical services.
Pitfall
Forgetting the outbound return rule results in one-way connectivity failures. Always pair inbound and outbound rules for expected flows.
Key Takeaway

Use NACLs for broad subnet filters and compliance controls, and ensure paired inbound/outbound rules due to their stateless nature.

screens.title: Security Groups and NACLs together: defense-in-depth
screens.narratorSegment: Defense-in-depth uses both Security Groups and NACLs to create overlapping protections so a misconfiguration in one layer does not cause catastrophic exposure. Security Groups should be your primary, stateful control for instances. Configure them to allow only required ports and prefer Security Group references for intra-VPC traffic. NACLs should provide a coarse-grained perimeter at the subnet level, enforcing deny-by-default policies where compliance requires it. A typical pattern: public web subnet has NACLs that permit HTTP and HTTPS and ephemeral outbound ports, while the web server Security Group allows inbound 80 and 443 and egress as necessary. The database subnet has a stricter NACL allowing only the application subnet CIDR and a database Security Group that references the application Security Group ID for the specific database port. A common misconception is that NACL denies will replace the need for Security Groups; they do not. Another mistake is duplicating overly permissive rules in both layers, which defeats the point of layered security. Example: if a NACL inadvertently allows a wide range of ports, a permissive Security Group could expose instances. Key takeaway: use NACLs for broad boundaries and Security Groups for specific, stateful permissions and always test both layers together.

keyIdea.text: NACLs set coarse subnet boundaries and Security Groups provide fine-grained, stateful instance controls — use both for resilience and compliance.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Defense-in-Depth
Pattern
Combine NACLs and Security Groups so each layer enforces different aspects of policy: broad subnet rules and narrow instance rules.
Example stack
Public subnet NACL allows 80/443; web SG allows 80/443 from internet. Private DB subnet NACL allows only app CIDR; DB SG allows only app SG ID on DB port.
Operational tip
Maintain a change checklist and test both layers after changes. Visualize reachability and use staging probes to validate both NACL and SG behavior before production rollout.
Misconception
Assuming one layer alone is sufficient. Layers complement each other and reduce the blast radius of a single misconfiguration.
Key Takeaway

Use NACLs and Security Groups together to enforce broad boundaries and fine permissions, and test them in concert.

screens.title: Hands-on: Hub-and-spoke for prod, dev, and shared-services
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the hands-on scenario: you will connect three VPCs — prod-vpc, dev-vpc, and shared-services-vpc — to a Transit Gateway so shared-services can reach both prod and dev, but prod and dev remain isolated from each other. Start by creating three VPCs with non-overlapping CIDRs, for example 10.1.0.0/16, 10.2.0.0/16, and 10.3.0.0/16. Create the Transit Gateway and then create attachments for each VPC, including at least one subnet ID per attachment. Next create two TGW route tables: SharedServices-TGW-RT and Isolation-TGW-RT. Associate the shared-services attachment with SharedServices-TGW-RT and propagate its routes. For isolation, associate prod and dev attachments with Isolation-TGW-RT and add a static route to shared-services CIDR that points to the shared-services attachment — or alternatively propagate shared-services into Isolation-TGW-RT while ensuring prod and dev are not propagated into SharedServices-TGW-RT. Update VPC route tables so that destinations for other VPC CIDRs go to the Transit Gateway. Finally test: from prod, attempt to reach dev — it should fail. From prod, reach shared-services — it should succeed. Document your associations and propagations so the design is reviewed and repeatable. Key takeaway: follow the attachment, route table, associate, propagate, and VPC-route update sequence, and validate isolation with controlled probes.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Hands-on Scenario
Tasks
  1. Create three VPCs with CIDRs 10.1.0.0/16, 10.2.0.0/16, 10.3.0.0/16.
  2. Create a Transit Gateway and attachments for each VPC.
  3. Create SharedServices-TGW-RT and Isolation-TGW-RT.
  4. Associate and propagate according to the isolation plan.
  5. Update VPC route tables to target the TGW for inter-VPC CIDRs.
Validation
Confirm prod cannot reach dev, but both can reach shared-services. Verify DNS and NTP remain reachable as needed.
Example mapping
SharedServices-TGW-RT: propagate shared-services; add static routes to prod and dev CIDRs. Isolation-TGW-RT: associate prod and dev; add static route to shared-services CIDR pointing to shared-services attachment.
Operational tip
Keep a runbook of associations and propagations. Mistakes in route table association are the most common cause of accidental cross-VPC access.
Key Takeaway

Plan, document, and validate your TGW associations and propagations. Test isolation with controlled probes before declaring success.

screens.title: CloudFormation starter: Transit Gateway and VPCs
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter includes a CloudFormation starter snippet that creates three VPCs, a Transit Gateway, and placeholders for Transit Gateway attachments and route table updates. The template defines the VPC resources with CIDR blocks and standard DNS support flags. The Transit Gateway resource is declared with a placeholder ASN. Attachments require actual subnet IDs from the created VPCs; in practice you should reference explicit subnet logical IDs that you create elsewhere in your template or import as parameters. The template includes an example of how to create a Transit Gateway attachment resource, but it leaves the TGW route tables and associations as comments — you must add those resources and the appropriate AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayRouteTable, TransitGatewayRouteTableAssociation, and TransitGatewayRouteTablePropagation resources. For VPC route table updates, the template shows a prototypical AWS::EC2::Route resource that needs a concrete RouteTableId and a DestinationCidrBlock pointing at the Transit Gateway. A common oversight is leaving CIDR destinations as 0.0.0.0/0; instead, scope routes to specific VPC CIDRs for inter-VPC traffic. When deploying at scale, break the template into modular stacks, pass subnet IDs and TGW IDs as parameters, and run changes in a staging account first. Key takeaway: the starter template is a scaffold — fill in concrete subnet IDs, TGW route tables, associations, propagations, and VPC route updates before deployment.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › CloudFormation Snippet
Starter snippet
A minimal scaffold creates three VPCs and the Transit Gateway resource. Attachments and route resources are placeholders that must be completed before deployment.
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: AWS Transit Gateway Hub and Spoke Network Setup

Resources:
  ProdVPC:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPC
    Properties:
      CidrBlock: 10.1.0.0/16
      EnableDnsSupport: true
      EnableDnsHostnames: true

  DevVPC:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPC
    Properties:
      CidrBlock: 10.2.0.0/16
      EnableDnsSupport: true
      EnableDnsHostnames: true

  SharedServicesVPC:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPC
    Properties:
      CidrBlock: 10.3.0.0/16
      EnableDnsSupport: true
      EnableDnsHostnames: true

  MyTransitGateway:
    Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGateway
    Properties:
      Description: Central Transit Gateway
      AmazonSideAsn: 64512

  # Attachments, TGW Route Tables, Associations, Propagations, and VPC Route Updates to be added
Deployment notes
Replace subnet placeholder IDs with concrete logical references or parameters. Add TransitGatewayRouteTable, Association, and Propagation resources. Update Route resources with correct RouteTableId values.
Common mistakes
  • Leaving 0.0.0.0/0 where specific VPC CIDRs are required for inter-VPC routes.
  • Forgetting TGW route table associations so attachments end up in default or wrong tables.
  • Not testing route updates in staging and breaking services like DNS or NTP.
Pro tip
Modularize template into nested stacks and pass TGW and subnet IDs as parameters to reduce blast radius and improve reuse.
Key Takeaway

Treat the snippet as a scaffold: fill attachments, TGW route tables, associations, propagations, and scoped VPC routes before production deployment.

screens.title: Common networking challenges and mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: Complex VPC environments introduce operational risks that show up as connectivity failures or unintended access. Common problems include incorrect TGW route table associations, forgotten VPC route updates, NACL misordering that blocks return traffic, and Security Groups that are too permissive or mis-scoped. A frequent operational pitfall is blocking DNS or NTP inadvertently when tightening NACLs or SGs; these services are widely used and can cause cascading failures if blocked. Mitigation starts with a testing discipline: make changes in a staging account and run reachability tests for critical services like DNS and NTP. Use AWS Network Manager or equivalent visualization tools to inspect TGW attachments and route propagation. When troubleshooting, follow a triage sequence: confirm attachments are in the expected TGW route table, verify propagation entries exist, check VPC route tables point to the TGW for targeted CIDRs, review NACL inbound/outbound pairs, and review Security Group rules for instance-level access. Use packet capture or reachability probes where allowed. Document rollback steps and keep a change runbook. Example: if app servers suddenly lose access to an internal logging service, verify TGW propagation and VPC routes before adjusting Security Groups. Key takeaway: adopt a repeatable validation sequence and never assume an attachment implies connectivity.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Troubleshooting
Triage Sequence
  1. Confirm TGW attachment and route table association.
  2. Verify TGW propagation entries for expected CIDRs.
  3. Check VPC route tables point to TGW for inter-VPC CIDRs.
  4. Inspect NACL inbound/outbound pairs for blocked ports.
  5. Review Security Group rules for instance-level permissions.
Operational safeguards
  • Make changes in staging; validate DNS and NTP before production.
  • Keep runbooks with rollback steps and test probes for critical paths.
  • Use visualization tools to detect unexpected propagation or associations.
Warning
Changing NACLs without matching outbound rules can silently break application responses. Always pair rules and test.
Key Takeaway

Validate changes methodically: attachments, propagation, VPC routes, NACLs, then Security Groups. Test DNS and NTP early.

screens.title: Design decisions: scale, isolation, and compliance
screens.narratorSegment: When architecting VPC networks for enterprises, trade-offs are inevitable. Aim for a consistent naming and tagging strategy so resources and TGW attachments are auditable. Choose CIDR blocks with future expansion and potential on-premise overlap in mind. Use a shared-services VPC for central capabilities like Active Directory or logging, and consider making that the only spoke that can reach multiple other VPCs through carefully configured TGW route tables. For compliance-sensitive workloads, place them in dedicated VPCs and apply restrictive NACLs at the subnet boundary combined with Security Groups that only allow known sources. Avoid too many small VPCs which increase operational burden; instead favor purpose-driven VPCs with predictable roles. Maintain a change control process for route and firewall updates and always run tests in non-production first. Finally, document network topology and keep TGW route table intent documented so future engineers understand why attachments are associated the way they are. Example decision: allocate fewer, well-documented VPCs and use Transit Gateway segmentation for controlled sharing instead of proliferating peering links. Key takeaway: make decisions intentionally with an eye to future growth, audits, and ease of operations.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll build a practical mental model for enterprise network design on AWS. You will learn why a flat single-VPC model breaks down as organizations grow, and how a hub-and-spoke Transit Gateway architecture reduces operational complexity while supporting isolation. We'll also unpack two complementary firewall primitives: Security Groups, which are stateful and instance-focused, and Network ACLs, which are stateless and subnet-focused. Throughout, you'll see concrete examples: separate VPCs for dev, staging, and production; a shared services VPC that exposes central services; and an isolation pattern that prevents direct east–west traffic between sensitive environments. I will highlight common mistakes — for example, relying only on Security Groups for subnet-level controls or creating a peering mesh that becomes unmanageable — and show how route tables and Transit Gateway route table associations and propagations enforce intended connectivity. By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain when Transit Gateway is the right choice, how to combine NACLs and Security Groups for defense-in-depth, and what checks to run after a change to avoid breaking DNS or time synchronization. Think about one network you manage now and whether a centralized hub could simplify its routing; that's the lens we use here.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when designing enterprise networks on AWS. First, you will learn to design multi-VPC architectures that provide clear isolation boundaries while remaining scalable. That means assigning VPCs roles, choosing CIDR ranges, and planning connectivity so teams don't create ad hoc peering meshes. Second, you will implement hub-and-spoke network topologies using AWS Transit Gateway. You will understand attachments, route tables, associations and propagations so the hub enforces traffic flows. Third, you will differentiate Security Groups and Network ACLs: when to use stateful, instance-level controls versus stateless, subnet-level deny-or-allow policies, and how to combine them for defense-in-depth. Fourth, you will identify and mitigate common networking challenges in complex VPC environments, such as unintended route propagation, broken DNS or NTP after policy changes, and overly permissive or overly fragmented VPC designs. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify you can design, implement, and validate secure, scalable networks. As you work through the hands-on scenario later, use these objectives to check that your architecture both enforces isolation and supports required shared services. Which objective feels most urgent for your current environment?

This second objectives slide links each skill to a demonstrable action. For multi-VPC design, you will specify CIDR ranges and assign each VPC a clear role such as production, development, or shared services. That reduces accidental overlap and eases routing. For Transit Gateway, you will create TGW attachments, configure two distinct TGW route tables — one for shared services and one for isolation — and use associations and propagations to control which spokes see which routes. For Security Groups versus NACLs, you will implement SGs that allow only necessary port access and NACLs that deny everything by default at the subnet boundary where compliance requires it. Finally, for mitigation, you will run an operational checklist after changes: confirm route table entries, verify DNS resolution and NTP, and test reachability with controlled probes in a staging environment. Each objective is designed to be checked with a hands-on task or a short test so you can prove the competency. As you move forward, use the hands-on scenario to practice these steps in sequence and verify that your design enforces the isolation goals.

Multi-VPC architecture is the deliberate use of multiple Virtual Private Clouds to provide isolation, organizational boundaries, and scale. Practically, that means creating VPCs with specific roles — for example production, development, and shared services — and assigning CIDR ranges so they do not overlap. A clear purpose for each VPC matters because it reduces accidental exposure; a production VPC will carry stricter rules than a development VPC. When planning CIDRs, reserve headroom for future subnets and avoid ranges that will conflict with on-prem networks if you plan to connect via VPN or Direct Connect. A common misconception is that more VPCs always equal better isolation; too many tiny VPCs without a connectivity strategy creates operational overhead. Conversely, one very large VPC can expose unrelated teams to risk and complicate compliance. A practical rule of thumb is to balance organizational boundaries with manageability: group tightly coupled workloads together, separate sensitive workloads into their own VPCs, and document CIDR allocations centrally. Example: allocate 10.1.0.0/16 to production, 10.2.0.0/16 to development, and 10.3.0.0/16 to shared services, leaving room to subnet them per availability zone. Key takeaway: design VPCs for clear purpose and future connectivity, not for ad hoc convenience. How would you split responsibilities across VPCs in your environment?

VPC peering is a lightweight way to connect two VPCs directly. It's easy to set up and useful for a small number of connections. But peering is non-transitive: if VPC A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B without an explicit peering connection. That non-transitive nature creates a combinatorial problem as you add VPCs. For N VPCs a full mesh requires N times N minus one over two peering links, and each new peering requires route table changes in both endpoints. In contrast, AWS Transit Gateway provides a central hub. Each VPC attaches to the Transit Gateway as a spoke, and the Transit Gateway manages inter-VPC routing with route tables, associations, and propagations. This is more scalable and simplifies policy enforcement. A misconception is that Transit Gateway automatically opens all communications; it does not. You still control connectivity via Transit Gateway route tables and VPC route table entries. Example: with three VPCs — prod, dev, shared-services — you can attach all three to a TGW and use two TGW route tables to allow shared-services to reach both prod and dev, while preventing direct traffic between prod and dev. Key takeaway: use peering for a few pairwise connections, and choose Transit Gateway when you need scale, central policy, and transitive connectivity management.

AWS Transit Gateway is a central hub where VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect gateways attach as spokes. Each attachment represents a connection between the Transit Gateway and a VPC or on-prem gateway. The gateway itself contains route tables; you create associations and propagations to control which attachments learn or receive which routes. Associations link attachments to a specific TGW route table, and propagation advertises routes from an attachment into a route table. This design allows you to create multiple TGW route tables for different traffic domains. For example, create a SharedServices-TGW-RT that propagates the shared-services attachment and associates that attachment with the table so the shared service is reachable. Create an Isolation-TGW-RT that associates prod and dev attachments, but only propagates routes to the shared-services attachment so prod and dev cannot reach each other directly. A common misconception is that attaching a VPC to the TGW automatically grants full connectivity; it does not. You must update both the TGW route table and the VPC route table to direct traffic to the Transit Gateway for inter-VPC communication. Example: to expose shared services to both spokes, propagate shared-services routes and add static routes for prod and dev CIDRs in the SharedServices-TGW-RT. Key takeaway: the combination of associations and propagations gives you flexible, central traffic control.

Configuring Transit Gateway routing is a four-step process you should treat as a deliberate workflow. Step one: create the Transit Gateway and attach each VPC by creating Transit Gateway attachments; each attachment must include subnet IDs from the VPC. Step two: create TGW route tables for the traffic patterns you require — for example, SharedServices-TGW-RT and Isolation-TGW-RT. Step three: associate attachments with the appropriate TGW route table and configure route propagations so routes from attachments appear where they should. Propagation is what advertises a spoke's CIDR into a TGW route table. Step four: update the route tables within each VPC to direct inter-VPC traffic to the Transit Gateway. If you forget this step, the TGW will not be used even though the attachment exists. A common pitfall is misconfiguring associations so attachments end up in the wrong TGW table, accidentally enabling transitive flows. Example flow: attach prod, dev, and shared-services; associate prod and dev to Isolation-TGW-RT; propagate shared-services into SharedServices-TGW-RT and add static routes to prod and dev CIDRs in SharedServices-TGW-RT. Finally, test connectivity using controlled probes and validate DNS resolution. Key takeaway: follow the attach, table, associate, propagate, and VPC-route update sequence to avoid partial connectivity.

Security Groups are a stateful virtual firewall applied to network interfaces and instances. When you allow inbound traffic on a port, the return traffic is automatically allowed back out — you do not need explicit outbound rules for responses unless you have tightened outbound policies. Security Groups are permissive by design: you allow specific traffic and everything else is implicitly denied. This makes them ideal for instance-level protection where you want granular control, for example allowing inbound TCP 80 and 443 to web servers. A common mistake is using Security Groups as the only line of defense for subnet-level isolation; they protect instances but do not replace subnet filters when compliance requires deny-by-default at the boundary. Best practice: attach Security Groups that allow minimal required ports and, when possible, reference other Security Groups rather than IPs for tighter intra-VPC controls. Example: web server SG allows 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0, and database SG allows MySQL from the web server SG ID only. Key takeaway: use Security Groups for precise, stateful instance protections and pair them with NACLs for broader subnet-level controls when needed.

Network Access Control Lists are stateless filters applied at the subnet boundary. They evaluate rules in numeric order from lowest to highest, and they support both allow and deny rules. Because they are stateless, you must create both inbound and outbound rules for request and response traffic. NACLs are deny-by-default when newly created, requiring explicit allows for everything you want. This makes them useful as a coarse-grained 'moat' around a subnet, especially for regulatory workloads that demand strong subnet-level boundaries. For example, to allow web traffic into a public subnet you would add inbound rules for TCP ports 80 and 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and outbound rules permitting ephemeral ports so the web server can respond. For a database subnet, you might add an inbound rule that allows only the application's subnet CIDR on the database port and deny everything else. A common mistake is misordering NACL rules or forgetting corresponding outbound entries, which will break connections unexpectedly. Use NACLs to enforce broad deny/allow policies and Security Groups to handle instance-level stateful controls. Key takeaway: NACLs provide a coarse, stateless defense at the subnet perimeter and are ideal for compliance-driven controls.

Defense-in-depth uses both Security Groups and NACLs to create overlapping protections so a misconfiguration in one layer does not cause catastrophic exposure. Security Groups should be your primary, stateful control for instances. Configure them to allow only required ports and prefer Security Group references for intra-VPC traffic. NACLs should provide a coarse-grained perimeter at the subnet level, enforcing deny-by-default policies where compliance requires it. A typical pattern: public web subnet has NACLs that permit HTTP and HTTPS and ephemeral outbound ports, while the web server Security Group allows inbound 80 and 443 and egress as necessary. The database subnet has a stricter NACL allowing only the application subnet CIDR and a database Security Group that references the application Security Group ID for the specific database port. A common misconception is that NACL denies will replace the need for Security Groups; they do not. Another mistake is duplicating overly permissive rules in both layers, which defeats the point of layered security. Example: if a NACL inadvertently allows a wide range of ports, a permissive Security Group could expose instances. Key takeaway: use NACLs for broad boundaries and Security Groups for specific, stateful permissions and always test both layers together.

Let's walk through the hands-on scenario: you will connect three VPCs — prod-vpc, dev-vpc, and shared-services-vpc — to a Transit Gateway so shared-services can reach both prod and dev, but prod and dev remain isolated from each other. Start by creating three VPCs with non-overlapping CIDRs, for example 10.1.0.0/16, 10.2.0.0/16, and 10.3.0.0/16. Create the Transit Gateway and then create attachments for each VPC, including at least one subnet ID per attachment. Next create two TGW route tables: SharedServices-TGW-RT and Isolation-TGW-RT. Associate the shared-services attachment with SharedServices-TGW-RT and propagate its routes. For isolation, associate prod and dev attachments with Isolation-TGW-RT and add a static route to shared-services CIDR that points to the shared-services attachment — or alternatively propagate shared-services into Isolation-TGW-RT while ensuring prod and dev are not propagated into SharedServices-TGW-RT. Update VPC route tables so that destinations for other VPC CIDRs go to the Transit Gateway. Finally test: from prod, attempt to reach dev — it should fail. From prod, reach shared-services — it should succeed. Document your associations and propagations so the design is reviewed and repeatable. Key takeaway: follow the attachment, route table, associate, propagate, and VPC-route update sequence, and validate isolation with controlled probes.

The chapter includes a CloudFormation starter snippet that creates three VPCs, a Transit Gateway, and placeholders for Transit Gateway attachments and route table updates. The template defines the VPC resources with CIDR blocks and standard DNS support flags. The Transit Gateway resource is declared with a placeholder ASN. Attachments require actual subnet IDs from the created VPCs; in practice you should reference explicit subnet logical IDs that you create elsewhere in your template or import as parameters. The template includes an example of how to create a Transit Gateway attachment resource, but it leaves the TGW route tables and associations as comments — you must add those resources and the appropriate AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayRouteTable, TransitGatewayRouteTableAssociation, and TransitGatewayRouteTablePropagation resources. For VPC route table updates, the template shows a prototypical AWS::EC2::Route resource that needs a concrete RouteTableId and a DestinationCidrBlock pointing at the Transit Gateway. A common oversight is leaving CIDR destinations as 0.0.0.0/0; instead, scope routes to specific VPC CIDRs for inter-VPC traffic. When deploying at scale, break the template into modular stacks, pass subnet IDs and TGW IDs as parameters, and run changes in a staging account first. Key takeaway: the starter template is a scaffold — fill in concrete subnet IDs, TGW route tables, associations, propagations, and VPC route updates before deployment.

Complex VPC environments introduce operational risks that show up as connectivity failures or unintended access. Common problems include incorrect TGW route table associations, forgotten VPC route updates, NACL misordering that blocks return traffic, and Security Groups that are too permissive or mis-scoped. A frequent operational pitfall is blocking DNS or NTP inadvertently when tightening NACLs or SGs; these services are widely used and can cause cascading failures if blocked. Mitigation starts with a testing discipline: make changes in a staging account and run reachability tests for critical services like DNS and NTP. Use AWS Network Manager or equivalent visualization tools to inspect TGW attachments and route propagation. When troubleshooting, follow a triage sequence: confirm attachments are in the expected TGW route table, verify propagation entries exist, check VPC route tables point to the TGW for targeted CIDRs, review NACL inbound/outbound pairs, and review Security Group rules for instance-level access. Use packet capture or reachability probes where allowed. Document rollback steps and keep a change runbook. Example: if app servers suddenly lose access to an internal logging service, verify TGW propagation and VPC routes before adjusting Security Groups. Key takeaway: adopt a repeatable validation sequence and never assume an attachment implies connectivity.

When architecting VPC networks for enterprises, trade-offs are inevitable. Aim for a consistent naming and tagging strategy so resources and TGW attachments are auditable. Choose CIDR blocks with future expansion and potential on-premise overlap in mind. Use a shared-services VPC for central capabilities like Active Directory or logging, and consider making that the only spoke that can reach multiple other VPCs through carefully configured TGW route tables. For compliance-sensitive workloads, place them in dedicated VPCs and apply restrictive NACLs at the subnet boundary combined with Security Groups that only allow known sources. Avoid too many small VPCs which increase operational burden; instead favor purpose-driven VPCs with predictable roles. Maintain a change control process for route and firewall updates and always run tests in non-production first. Finally, document network topology and keep TGW route table intent documented so future engineers understand why attachments are associated the way they are. Example decision: allocate fewer, well-documented VPCs and use Transit Gateway segmentation for controlled sharing instead of proliferating peering links. Key takeaway: make decisions intentionally with an eye to future growth, audits, and ease of operations.

Here are three compact ideas to carry forward. First, multi-VPC architecture organizes networks by role and sensitivity; plan CIDR ranges and VPC responsibilities to avoid collisions and reduce risk. Second, AWS Transit Gateway is a scalable hub that avoids peering mesh complexity; use associations and propagations in TGW route tables to control who sees which routes. Third, Security Groups and NACLs are complementary: Security Groups are stateful, instance-level controls, while NACLs are stateless, subnet-level filters useful for deny-by-default compliance. Keep these concepts in mind when designing networks and build a checklist to validate route and firewall changes. Which of these three will change how you design your next network?
